The coordinator selects and manages workers and worktrees.\\n\\n## Definition of Done\\n\\n- **Masih is the sole arbiter of truth.** CI, compilation, tests, and agent claims are evidence, not functional acceptance.\\n- Before important or difficult implementation work, turn the request into an explicit acceptance harness and confirm it with Masih.\\n- Implement, run the required automated checks, build/install when applicable, and hand Masih a plain user test checklist.\\n- A task becomes verified only after Masih accepts the user-visible behavior and the evidence is recorded in `TASKS.md`.\\n- Behavior must be implemented, not merely documented.\\n- Rust changes pass the applicable Rust checks. This repository contains no Python.\\n- Known gaps and skipped checks are stated plainly.\\n\\n## Evals First\\n\\nBehavior that can silently do nothing needs an eval before it is changed. Every behavioral eval needs a positive case and a negative case, and the eval must be shown capable of failing before it is trusted.\\n\\nPrefer behavioral evidence over plumbing-only tests: plant something only the feature could know or produce, run the real path, assert that it arrives, then disable or break the feature and assert that it does not.\\n\\n## Known Gap: Durable Memory Promotion\\n\\nMemory extraction and phase-2 processing run, but real-machine promotion into `MEMORY.md` has not been demonstrated. Promotion currently requires `recall_count >= 3` and `unique_query_count >= 2`, and real usage has not reached that gate reliably.\\n\\nDo not change the promotion gate or memory default without Masih's explicit approval. Memory ships off. Anything claiming durable memory works must show a real promotion commit in `~/.elpis/memories/.git`; passing plumbing tests is insufficient.\\n\\n## Agent Dispatch\\n\\nUse one coordinator and one worktree per implementation task. The coordinator owns `GUIDE.md`, `TASKS.md`, architecture decisions, task ordering, integration, and final acceptance. Workers implement bounded tasks; they do not redefine the product.\\n\\nDo not run two agents against the same files or an unresolved shared interface. More agents increase speed only when tasks are genuinely independent.\\n\\nFor deterministic multi-agent work graphs, follow `docs/WORK_GRAPHS.md`.\\n\\n### Difficulty Routing\\n\\n| Difficulty | Characteristics | Preferred worker |\\n| --- | --- | --- |\\n| Easy | One localized behavior, known solution, low-risk change, narrow test | Fast low-cost worker |\\n| Medium | Several files, bounded design choice, adaptation of an existing pattern | Balanced worker |\\n| Hard | Architecture, runtime ownership, security, permissions, context/memory semantics, migration, cross-cutting interfaces | Main high-reasoning model |\\n\\nEscalate when investigation reveals a broader interface or product decision. Do not let a worker quietly expand scope.\\n\\n### Worktree Workflow\\n\\n1. Start from the shared committed control baseline.\\n2. Select the Current Action from `TASKS.md` after verifying dependencies.\\n3. Create one branch and worktree for that task.\\n4. Give the worker exact scope, non-goals, dependencies, acceptance criteria, and required checks.\\n5. Require changed files, checks run, evidence, risks, and commit hash.\\n6. Review and integrate one branch at a time; rerun the acceptance check after integration.\\n7. The coordinator alone updates feature status to `verified` after Masih accepts it.\\n\\nRemove a worktree only after its branch is integrated or intentionally abandoned.\\n\\n### Worker Prompt Contract\\n\\nEvery delegated prompt must contain:\\n\\n```text\\nTask ID:\\nDesired user-visible behavior:\\nWhy it is needed:\\nAllowed files:\\nForbidden scope:\\nDependencies already verified:\\nAcceptance test:\\nRequired checks:\\nReturn: summary, changed files, verification, risks, commit hash.\\n```\\n\\nIf any field is missing or contradictory, challenge the requirement before coding.\\n"}]

[{"type":"input_text","text":"Script completed\\nWall time 0.2 seconds\\nOutput:\\n"},{"type":"input_text","text":"# Elpis Context Sovereignty & 4-Layer Pruning Pipeline\\n\\nElpis enforces **Context Sovereignty**: the principle that context is a strictly budgeted working set, not a dumped chat transcript. The user maintains live visibility and explicit control over every byte admitted to the agent's context window.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 1. Systemic Role in Elpis\\n\\nContext management acts as the primary gatekeeper between raw workspace/session events and the active model inference loop:\\n\\n```text\\n[User Prompt / Task Input]\\n           |\\n           v\\n+----------+-------------------------------------------------------+\\n|                 ELPIS CONTEXT ADMISSION GATE                     |\\n|  - GOAL.md (Active Goal)       - ES.md (Executive Summary)       |\\n|  - MEMORY.md (Curated Facts)   - AGENTS.md / Skill Rules         |\\n|  - Context Ledger Selections   - Admitted @file references       |\\n+----------+-------------------------------------------------------+\\n           |\\n           v\\n+----------+-------------------------------------------------------+\\n|                    3-LAYER PRUNING PIPELINE                      |\\n|  Layer 1: RTK Shell-Output Filter (Pre-model command rewrite)   |\\n|  Layer 2: Deterministic Safety Cap (Upper bound truncation)     |\\n|  Layer 3: Ace Pressure Cycle (30% used trigger, 20% used target) |\\n+----------+-------------------------------------------------------+\\n           |\\n           v\\n+----------+-------------------------------------------------------+\\n|                 MODEL INFERENCE (Selected Provider)              |\\n+------------------------------------------------------------------+\\n```\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 2. The 4-Layer Pruning Pipeline\\n\\nLong agent sessions accumulate dead ends, voluminous search results, and repetitive file reads. Elpis separates **working context** from **durable evidence**.\\n\\n```text\\n[Raw Tool / Terminal Output]\\n           |\\n           v\\n[Layer 1: RTK Filter]          -> Pre-model: compacts verbose CLI output (rg, find).\\n           |\\n           v\\n[Layer 2: Safety Cap]          -> Pre-model: Hard deterministic upper-bound truncation.\\n           |\\n           v\\n[Active Agent Turn Execution]  -> Tool outputs remain verbatim during active turn.\\n           |\\n           v\\n[Layer 3: Ace Pressure Cycle]  -> Between follow-ups: at 70% remaining, reclaims toward 80%,\\n                                  then holds off until use regrows to 70% remaining again.\\n           |\\n           v\\n[Native /compact]              -> Fallback only, when no layer can reclaim anything further.\\n```\\n\\nLayer 3 is a single trigger, run as a gated cycle rather than continuously. An earlier\\n\\"steady\\" trigger also fired on backlog size alone, independently of how full the window was;\\nit was removed because it produced runs of tiny passes inside the healthy 20-30% band, and\\nevery pass discards the reusable prompt-cache prefix past its first rewritten item. The case\\nit was meant to cover -- a single turn that balloons past the boundary without ever ending --\\nis already handled here, because the eligible region is cut by recency rather than at a turn\\nboundary. See `cache-friendly-pruning.md`.\\n\\n### Pipeline Layer Comparison\\n\\n| Layer | Trigger | Scope | Behavior | Failure Recovery |\\n| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |\\n| **1. RTK Filter** | Tool execution | Shell output (`rg`, `git status`, `find`) | Compacts raw command output using pattern filters before the agent sees it. | Fallback to unfiltered output on tool error. |\\n| **2. Safety Cap** | Tool execution | All raw tool outputs | Hard-truncates exceptionally large output blobs to protect context limits. Inherited from Codex, unchanged. | Preserves header & footer with truncation notice. |\\n| **3. Ace Pressure Cycle** | Exact model-window use reaches 30% (70% remaining), and a previous cycle has since been seen below 30% | Oldest eligible tool exploration, including the turn still running, but never a sealed epoch | Selects only enough old tool evidence to target roughly 20% use (80% remaining); the newest 10% of the window stays verbatim. Useful results become a compact conclusion plus an evidence pointer; dead ends leave working context entirely. It reaches into the current turn, because a single tool-driven turn can cross the boundary without ever ending. One cycle gets at most 2 Ace passes, spent back to back; the cycle then closes and cannot reopen until use has been measured below 30% and has climbed back to it. Each applied pass seals its region with an epoch marker that later passes may not touch. | A failed pass changes nothing. Once the cycle's 2-pass budget is spent, or when nothing reclaimable remains at this boundary, Elpis requests native compaction rather than let the window drift toward the model's hard limit. |\\n\\n**All three layers ship with Elpis.** Layer 1 runs through RTK, which is a separate binary: `scripts/install-elpis.sh` installs it alongside Elpis (skip with `ELPIS_SKIP_RTK=1`), and on a launch that finds `rtk` on `PATH` with no `~/.elpis/hooks.json` of your own, Elpis writes the `PreToolUse` hook that calls `rtk hook claude`. It then passes the normal startup hook review before it can run. An existing `hooks.json` is never modified, so `{\\"hooks\\":{}}` opts out permanently, and Elpis's hook runtime (`codex-rs/hooks/src/events/pre_tool_use.rs`) is what accepts RTK's rewrite response.\\n\\nThe Ace pass runs between model follow-ups as well as at the end of a turn, so one\\nlong-running tool-driven turn cannot skip the trigger. Each pass records which\\ntrigger fired (`manual` or `pressure`) in its manifest and report. OpenAI-backed passes use\\nLuna at low reasoning effort. Every successful pass immediately recomputes the working\\nhistory estimate and writes `prune_report.md` alongside the session logs\\n(`codex-rs/core/src/session/context_prune_audit.rs`).\\nThe pass may run during a current turn, but it only receives and rewrites tool evidence\\nfrom earlier completed turns; current-turn observations remain intact for the next\\nfollow-up.\\n\\n`/prune` runs the Ace pass on demand across eligible tool evidence from completed turns.\\nIt keeps user and assistant messages, the current turn, and durable rollout evidence.\\n`/compact` is Elpis-owned conservative cleanup. It first runs the audited tool-evidence\\npass, then asks Luna Max to mark older whole conversation messages as `KEEP` or `DELETE`.\\nThe latest turn is protected; kept content is copied verbatim; incomplete, malformed, or\\nuncertain decisions leave conversation history unchanged. A successful deletion starts a\\nnew window while the raw transcript remains intact. An explicit custom `compact_prompt`\\nretains the upstream summary path as an opt-out. The Context Ledger's exact used-token\\nnumber is authoritative after either path.\\n\\n### Ace pass audit trail\\n\\nEvery applied Ace pass writes an immutable audit before the working history changes. If that audit cannot be written, Elpis keeps the working history and does not record the pass as applied.\\n\\n```text\\n~/.elpis/logs/\\n├── prune_report.md              # points at the latest pass; contains clickable file:// links\\n└── pruning/passes/<pass-id>/\\n    ├── ace.json                 # Ace's exact instructions, input, and raw response\\n    ├── manifest.json            # every reviewed call ID and its kept/deleted decision\\n    └── items/*.json             # exact model-visible before/after for one call\\n```\\n\\nYou do not have to go looking for these: `prune_report.md` renders `ace.json` and `manifest.json` as clickable links (`context_prune_audit.rs`). The audit deliberately omits the system prompt, skills, and transcript, so it stays readable.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 3. Context Lifetimes\\n\\nEvery item admitted into Elpis context carries an explicit lifetime:\\n\\n```text\\n+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+\\n| DURABLE LIFETIME                                                                 |\\n| - AGENTS.md rules, active GOAL.md, MEMORY.md, explicit user constraints           |\\n+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+\\n                                         |\\n                                         v\\n+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+\\n| TASK LIFETIME                                                                     |\\n| - Decisions, changed file paths, blockers, verification, ES.md checkpoint         |\\n+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+\\n                                         |\\n                                         v\\n+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+\\n| TURN LIFETIME (Expires after turn question is answered)                           |\\n| - Terminal reads, searches, directory listings, command probes, temporary diffs   |\\n+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+\\n```\\n\\n1. **Durable:** Survives across compaction, model switches, and restarts.\\n2. **Task:** Survives across turn execution within the current task; summarized into `ES.md` upon task transition.\\n3. **Turn:** Expires immediately after the active turn question is answered. Raw output is evicted from working context, leaving behind an exact evidence pointer (rollout ID / log path).\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 4. Context Ledger (`Tab` / `Alt+C`) & `admission.toml`\\n\\nElpis provides interactive context admission control in the TUI:\\n\\n- **Context Ledger Panel (`Tab` or `Alt+C`):** A side panel shown by default, listing every admitted portable context source with exact byte sizes and the percentage of the model context window in use. It is 52 columns wide, narrowing to a proportional slice on smaller terminals so the composer keeps room. While a turn is running, `Tab` defers to the composer's queue-the-draft action; `Alt+C` always toggles the ledger.\\n- **`admission.toml` Control:** Toggling a row in the ledger writes `~/.elpis/context/workspaces/<workspace>/admission.toml`, which dynamically governs next-turn admission for:\\n  - `GOAL.md` (Active Goal)\\n  - `ES.md` (Executive Summary)\\n  - Global & project-level `AGENTS.md` rules\\n  - Individual portable development rules installed by Elpis\\n    (`~/.elpis/skills/dev/*.md`)\\n\\nElpis embeds and installs its portable development rules on first launch and refreshes\\nthe managed files when the binary changes. The installed directory is the single default\\nsource; a project-sibling `skills/dev` is not scanned, so a development checkout cannot\\ndouble-admit the same rules. Machine-specific additions remain opt-in through\\n`ELPIS_DEV_SKILLS_DIRS`.\\n\\n![The Context Ledger listing admitted instruction files with their token counts and included state](assets/context-ledger.png)\\n\\n### `/context` — where the window went\\n\\nThe ledger answers *what is admitted*. `/context` answers *what filled the window*: token\\nusage as a grid broken down by category — user messages, agent responses, tool calls,\\nsystem prompt, skills, and free space — alongside the backtrack checkpoints available via\\n`Esc Esc`. The two are separate surfaces and neither replaces the other.\\n\\n![/context showing token usage as a grid, broken down by category, with available backtrack checkpoints](assets/elpis-context-slash.png)\\n\\n### Context Accounting Contract\\n\\nElpis exposes **one single source of truth** for context measurement:\\n\\n- Displayed percentages explicitly state whether they mean **used** or **remaining**.\\n- The percentage is computed against the model's own context window — used tokens over context window (`codex-rs/tui/src/chatwidget/context_ledger.rs`) — never against transcript length.\\n- It is reported in the Context Ledger. The persistent identity header carries product, model, and location only (`Elpis · model {model} · location {cwd}`); the inherited footer status line is deliberately suppressed so there is exactly one place to read the number.\\n- `/usage` enumerates admitted sources, byte sizes, and lifetime reasons.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 5. Systemic Inter-Dependencies\\n\\n- **Integration with Sessions:** the admitted `GOAL.md` and `ES.md` sources are exactly what lean continuation carries into a fresh thread; see [Sessions](sessions.md).\\n- **Integration with Memory:** durable memory is a separate subsystem. It reads completed rollout transcripts from disk rather than hooking into compaction, so it does not depend on when a thread compacts. A `PreCompact` hook event is available if you want to run your own work at that moment. \\n- **Integration with Providers:** admitted context is normalized across provider wire formats while evidence pointers are preserved; see [Providers](providers.md).\\n"}]

[{"type":"input_text","text":"Script completed\\nWall time 0.2 seconds\\nOutput:\\n"},{"type":"input_text","text":"# Cache-friendly pruning\\n\\nWhy Elpis's context pruning is organised into **cycles** and **epochs**, and what that buys\\nthe prompt cache. Companion to `docs/context.md` (what pruning does) and\\n`docs/prompt-caching.md` (how the cache is addressed).\\n\\n## The old behaviour\\n\\nTwo triggers could start an automatic Ace pass:\\n\\n- **pressure** — active use reached 30% of the window; reclaim down toward 20%.\\n- **steady** — completed turns held ≥5% of the window in uncovered tool output. This one\\n  did not look at how full the window was at all.\\n\\nSteady is what made passes frequent. In the healthy 20–30% band a working agent produces\\nseveral percent of the window in tool output per turn, so steady re-armed almost as fast as\\nit was satisfied, and the automatic check runs twice per turn (once before the request, once\\nafter sampling). One measured session ran **42 applied passes over 103 requests**, most of\\nthem reclaiming a small increment.\\n\\nA budget of two passes per *pressure crossing* existed, but steady was never budgeted, so it\\nwas not a bound on total passes.\\n\\n## Why that cost cache reuse\\n\\nThe Responses API caches a **prefix**. A request reads from cache only up to the first byte\\nthat differs from a previously *written* prefix.\\n\\nPruning rewrites the oldest rewritable items — that is the point of it — so every pass\\ninvalidates the prompt from its first rewritten item onward. Ordinary turns only append, so\\nbetween passes the prefix is stable and hits; each pass is a cliff.\\n\\nTwo things made the cliff worse than it had to be:\\n\\n1. **42 cliffs.** Frequency alone dominates.\\n2. **Nothing had ever been written at the surviving boundary.** Implicit caching writes one\\n   breakpoint near the end of each prompt. After a pass, all of those sit past the point of\\n   divergence and are useless, so the request falls back to the newest entry that happens to\\n   predate the divergence — in the measured session, the 17,152-token initial prefix. It hit\\n   that plateau 43 times.\\n\\nPoint 2 is the important one: the region *before* the divergence was already large and\\nalready stable. It just was not a cache entry.\\n\\n## New behaviour: cycles with hysteresis\\n\\nAutomatic pruning now runs as a gated cycle (`PruneCycle` in `core/src/context_pruner.rs`):\\n\\n```\\nArmed  --(use >= 30%, pass applied)-->  Open{passes}\\nOpen   --(target reached | budget spent | nothing reclaimable)-->  Cooling\\nCooling --(use seen < 30%, then use >= 30%)-->  Armed\\n```\\n\\n- **Trigger** stays 30% used, **target** stays ~20% used.\\n- **Steady is gone.** Backlog size no longer starts a pass. The case it existed for — a\\n  single tool-driven turn ballooning without ever ending — is already covered by pressure,\\n  whose eligible region is cut by recency rather than at a turn boundary.\\n- A cycle may spend up to `MAX_PRESSURE_PRUNE_PASSES_PER_CYCLE` (2) passes **back to back**,\\n  because one pass is capped at `MAX_PRUNE_BATCH_TOKENS` and on a large window that can be\\n  less than the 30%→20% distance. Those are one logical cycle finishing its descent, not\\n  separate cycles.\\n- `Cooling` blocks every automatic pass. `run_context_prune` returns before it even selects\\n  a batch, so the 20–30% band cannot produce a pass of any kind.\\n\\nThe resulting shape is `20% → work → 21…29% → 30% → one cycle → 20% → work`.\\n\\n### The invariant\\n\\n> After a cycle closes, no automatic pass may run until measured use has been observed\\n> **below** the 30% trigger and has then climbed back **up to** it.\\n\\nBoth halves are required, and they are mutually exclusive within a single observation, so a\\ncooling cycle always spans at least two measurements on opposite sides of the boundary.\\n\\nThe \\"below first\\" half is not redundant. A cycle can also close *while still in pressure* —\\nbudget spent, or nothing left to reclaim. There `use >= 30%` is trivially true, so a\\ntrigger-only test would re-arm on the very next step and restore the old nibbling. For *why* the pruning layer is shaped the way it is, see\\n`docs/cache-friendly-pruning.md`.\\n\\n## Implicit vs explicit\\n\\nThe Responses API caches a *prefix* of the prompt. The prefix is `instructions`, then\\n`tools`, then `input` up to a breakpoint. A later request whose prefix is byte-identical up\\nto that breakpoint reads it from cache instead of paying full input price.\\n\\n**Implicit** (`prompt_cache_options` omitted, the API default): the server places one\\nbreakpoint on the latest message **and honours any explicit breakpoints the request\\ncarries**. That combination is what Elpis uses.\\n\\n**Explicit** (`prompt_cache_options.mode = \\"explicit\\"`): the automatic latest-message\\nbreakpoint is *disabled* and only the breakpoints the request carries are used.\\n\\nA breakpoint is a `prompt_cache_breakpoint: {\\"mode\\": \\"explicit\\"}` marker on a content\\nblock — the marker is named \\"explicit\\" in both modes:\\n\\n```json\\n{\\n  \\"model\\": \\"gpt-5.6-sol\\",\\n  \\"prompt_cache_key\\": \\"019fe741-dc08-7151-8706-71ead8fcceb8\\",\\n  \\"prompt_cache_options\\": { \\"mode\\": \\"explicit\\" },\\n  \\"input\\": [\\n    {\\n      \\"type\\": \\"message\\",\\n      \\"role\\": \\"user\\",\\n      \\"content\\": [\\n        { \\"type\\": \\"input_text\\", \\"text\\": \\"…\\",\\n          \\"prompt_cache_breakpoint\\": { \\"mode\\": \\"explicit\\" } }\\n      ]\\n    }\\n  ]\\n}\\n```\\n\\nConstraints that shape everything below:\\n\\n- Breakpoints are valid **only** on `input_text`, `input_image`, and `input_file` blocks.\\n  Reasoning items, tool calls, and tool outputs — the bulk of an agent transcript — cannot\\n  carry one.\\n- A request may create at most **four** new cache writes. In implicit mode the automatic\\n  latest-message breakpoint uses one, leaving three for explicit ones. Reads consider the\\n  latest 50 breakpoints, so entries from earlier turns can still hit.\\n- Explicit mode with **zero** breakpoints disables prompt caching for that request\\n  entirely, and is therefore strictly worse than implicit.\\n- GPT-5.6+ caches prefixes of **at least 1,024 tokens**. Below that a breakpoint is inert.\\n- `prompt_cache_options` and `prompt_cache_breakpoint` are **rejected** by models before\\n  GPT-5.6.\\n\\n## Elpis's cache boundary\\n\\nBreakpoints are gated two ways, both of which must hold:\\n\\n1. the provider is OpenAI, and\\n2. the model slug parses as `gpt-<major>.<minor>` at or past `5.6` (`gpt-5.6-sol`,\\n   `gpt-5.6-terra`, `gpt-5.6-luna`, and later families).\\n\\nWithin that gate they ship **on by default**: they ride alongside the server's implicit\\nbreakpoint rather than replacing it, so they can only add cache reads.\\n\\n`core/src/prompt_cache.rs` places up to two positions:\\n\\n- **Stable prefix** — the last eligible block in the leading run of instruction and\\n  tool-definition items (`AdditionalTools` and `Message` items, i.e. the developer\\n  instructions, AGENTS.md, and the opening user turn). The run ends at the first reasoning\\n  item, tool call, or assistant message. Nothing rewrites items in that run, so this is the\\n  floor every request can fall back to.\\n- **Frozen epoch boundary** — the newest context-pruning epoch marker\\n  (`context_pruner::frozen_prefix_len`). A pruning pass rewrites only what comes *after*\\n  it, so this entry survives the pass that invalidates everything else. Before the first\\n  pass it resolves to the stable prefix and dedupes away.\\n\\nThe **rolling tail** is deliberately *not* pinned on the default path: the server writes\\nthat breakpoint itself, and duplicating it would spend one of the four per-request writes\\nfor nothing. It is added only in explicit mode, where the automatic one is gone.\\n\\nIf no eligible block exists, no breakpoints and no `prompt_cache_options` are sent at all\\nand the server stays on implicit — never explicit-with-no-breakpoints.\\n\\nThe marker is stamped at serialization time (`codex_api::encode_responses_request`), not\\nstored on `ContentItem`. `ContentItem` is a persisted history type; a request-only cache\\nmarker must not end up in rollouts.\\n\\n### Why implicit rather than explicit\\n\\nExplicit mode is available behind `Feature::ExplicitPromptCache` (`explicit_prompt_cache` in\\nconfig, **off by default**) and is not recommended. Per the current API documentation,\\nimplicit mode already honours the breakpoints a request carries, so switching to explicit\\nbuys no additional placement — it only *removes* the free latest-message write and forces\\nElpis to reproduce it out of its own four-write budget. There is no serialized request shape\\nhere where explicit wins.\\n\\nAn earlier revision of this document assumed explicit mode was required to place\\nbreakpoints at all. It is not.\\n\\nOn the websocket incremental path, where a request sends only the delta and refers to the\\nrest via `previous_response_id`, both the options and the breakpoints are dropped: the\\npositions index the full input and no longer address anything.\\n\\n## `prompt_cache_key`\\n\\nThe key routes a request to the machine holding its cache. It does not itself invalidate\\nanything.\\n\\n- **Turn requests** use the bare session id. It is fixed for the life of the session, so\\n  pruning, compaction, and every other history rewrite leave it untouched. Only the prefix\\n  changes, which is exactly what the cache is meant to notice.\\n- **Background requests that reuse the session's client** get their own namespace:\\n  `<session-id>:context-prune` and `<session-id>:memory`. Their prefix is unrelated to the\\n  conversation, so sharing the turn's slot could only evict the turn prefix for no possible\\n  hit. Each namespace is itself constant per session and kind.\\n- A `prompt_cache_key` override (guardian review sessions) still wins over both.\\n\\n## Cache-write accounting\\n\\n`usage.input_tokens_details.cache_write_tokens` is parsed from the Responses stream. It is\\nnever inferred.\\n\\n`TokenUsage::cache_write_tokens` is `Option<i64>`:\\n\\n- `None` — the provider did not report the field. Every model before GPT-5.6, and every\\n  usage record written before this field existed.\\n- `Some(0)` — the provider reported a genuine zero.\\n\\nKeep the distinction when analysing runs: \\"no cache writes\\" and \\"cache writes not\\nmeasurable\\" are different findings. `TokenUsage::cache_write()` flattens to a number where\\nonly display or arithmetic matters.\\n\\nAccumulation stays `None` only while neither side ever reported the field; once one request\\ndoes, the running total is a number and later silent requests add nothing.\\n\\n`input_tokens` remains the provider's **total** input. `cached_input_tokens` and\\n`cache_write_tokens` are breakdowns *of* it, not additions *to* it — nothing sums them into\\ninput.\\n\\nThe field flows to the rollout `token_count` records, the pruning audit archive\\n(`~/.elpis/logs/pruning/`), and the `rollout-trace` inference records. It is **not** carried\\nby the app-server `TokenUsageBreakdown` wire type, so the TUI status card does not show it;\\nextending that type means regenerating its TypeScript and JSON schema artifacts.\\n\\n## How pruning interacts with cached prefixes\\n\\nA pruning pass rewrites the oldest rewritable items, so every prefix past its first\\nrewritten item diverges. **No breakpoint can prevent that** — removing content from the\\nmiddle of a prompt changes every prefix after it. Two things are done about it instead, both\\ndescribed in `docs/cache-friendly-pruning.md`:\\n\\n1. **Prune far less often.** Automatic pruning runs as a hysteresis cycle: 30% used → one\\n   cycle → ~20% used → no further pass until use regrows to 30%. The backlog-sized \\"steady\\"\\n   trigger, which fired independently of how full the window was, is gone.\\n2. **Raise the floor each pass falls back to.** Each applied pass seals its region with a\\n   byte-stable epoch marker and a breakpoint is placed on it, so the *next* pass falls back\\n   to that boundary instead of to the initial prefix.\\n\\n### The measurement that motivated this\\n\\nSession `019fe741` (2026-08-09, `gpt-5.6-sol`), before either change:\\n\\n| | |\\n|---|---|\\n| requests | 103 |\\n| applied pruning passes | 42 |\\n| overall cached-input rate | 62.8% (4.32M of 6.88M input tokens) |\\n| requests falling back to the 17,152-token stable prefix | 43 |\\n| requests with cached input under 30k | 47 |\\n\\nThe `cached = 17,152` plateau appears exactly 43 times — once per pruning event. That number\\n*is* the stable prefix (instructions + tools + initial context bundle). The region between\\nthat prefix and the divergence point was already large and already stable across passes;\\nit simply had never been *written* as a cache entry, because implicit caching only writes\\nnear the end of each prompt. The epoch breakpoint is what makes that region an entry.\\n\\n**Both effects are predictions, not results.** No run has been made against the new\\nlayout. See \\"What to inspect\\" below for how to check.\\n\\n## What to inspect\\n\\nPer request, from the rollout `token_count` records:\\n\\n- `input_tokens` — total input billed.\\n- `cached_input_tokens` — the part that hit. Divide by `input_tokens` for the hit rate.\\n- `cache_write_tokens` — the part written this request. `null` means unreported, not zero.\\n\\nSignals worth watching:\\n\\n- **A repeating low `cached_input_tokens` value** is a prefix invalidation, and its value\\n  tells you where the surviving boundary is. Correlate the count against\\n  `elpis.context-prune.v1:` checkpoints in the rollout.\\n- **The plateau value should now climb over a session.** Each pruning event should fall back\\n  to the newest epoch boundary, not to a fixed initial prefix. A *constant* plateau across\\n  many passes means the epoch breakpoint is not being written — check that the frozen prefix\\n  exceeds 1,024 tokens and that the marker is present in the request body.\\n- **The number of pruning events should be roughly (peak use − 20%) / 10% per session**, not\\n  one per turn. Count `\\"trigger\\": \\"pressure\\"` manifests in `~/.elpis/logs/pruning/passes/`.\\n- **`cached_input_tokens: 0` on pruning calls** is expected: each pruning batch is unique\\n  content, so it can never hit. The namespaced key keeps that miss from costing the turn\\n  loop its slot.\\n- **A prefix under 1,024 tokens** never caches on GPT-5.6, so a small stable prefix is\\n  worth nothing whichever mode is on.\\n\\n## Enabling explicit mode\\n\\n```toml\\n[features]\\nexplicit_prompt_cache = true\\n```\\n\\nThis switches `prompt_cache_options.mode` to `\\"explicit\\"` and adds a rolling-tail\\nbreakpoint to replace the automatic one it disables. It affects only GPT-5.6+ requests to\\nOpenAI, and it is **not** needed to get Elpis's breakpoints — those ship on by default. See\\n\\"Why implicit rather than explicit\\" above; keep it off unless a paired run shows otherwise.\\n"}]

\\n\\n\\n\\n# Never lose the thread.\\n\\n**You run an agent inside Elpis, and it becomes Elpis.**\\n\\nMore **QUALITY**. More **QUANTITY**.\\n\\n[![Linux verification](https://img.shields.io/github/actions/workflow/status/MasihMoafi/Elpis/embedded-elpis-linux.yml?branch=main&label=verification&style=flat-square)](https://github.com/MasihMoafi/Elpis/actions/workflows/embedded-elpis-linux.yml)\\n[![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-Apache%202.0-blue?style=flat-square)](LICENSE)\\n[![Telemetry](https://img.shields.io/badge/telemetry-off%20by%20default-brightgreen?style=flat-square)](#privacy-and-ownership)\\n\\n[Install](#quickstart) • [Features](#core-features) • [Docs](#documentation)\\n\\n
\\n\\n## Quickstart\\n\\nLinux x86_64 and macOS on Apple Silicon:\\n\\n```bash\\ncurl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MasihMoafi/Elpis/main/scripts/install-elpis.sh | bash && ~/.local/bin/elpis\\n```\\n\\nThe installer picks the right binary for your machine and also installs\\n[RTK](https://github.com/rtk-ai/rtk), which powers shell-output filtering. On first launch,\\nchoose a provider and sign in or enter its API key.\\n\\n`v0.1.2` is the current release.\\n\\n## What is Elpis\\n\\nThe agent runs the model loop. Elpis owns everything around it: context, memory, continuity, retrieval, permissions, and provider choice.\\n\\nSwap the agent and it inherits the same environment. Nothing about your project has to be explained twice.\\n\\nDifferent paths. Same roots. One shared project.\\n\\n## Why Elpis\\n\\nLong sessions fill up with transcripts, file reads, searches, and dead ends. Agents consume massive token budgets and execute dense sequences of tool calls to gather context—most of which is redundant and unnecessary. What matters gets buried in the story of how the agent got there, and every request pays for it.\\n\\n![Agents using excessive tool calls and tokens to gather redundant context](docs/assets/showcase-of-how-much-tool-calls.png)\\n\\nElpis keeps the two apart. The next request gets a small working set you can inspect. The full record stays on disk and is fetched only when it is needed.\\n\\n![Context trajectory](docs/assets/context-remaining-trajectory-band.svg)\\n\\n![Context retention](docs/assets/context-remaining-benchmark.svg)\\n\\n![Per-persona context](docs/assets/context-remaining-second-run.svg)\\n\\nThe screenshots below are historical examples of the same prompt in Elpis and Codex.\\nThe original per-run records were not preserved.\\n\\nA pinned, synthetic 3×10 comparison for exact recall, paraphrased recall, and negative\\ncontrols is specified in\\n[docs/evals/context-continuity](docs/evals/context-continuity/README.md). It has a\\ndeterministic scorer, but no score is published because the required provider runs and\\nraw transcripts have not been produced.\\n\\n
\\nHistorical screenshots\\n\\nStart:\\n\\n![Starting Elpis](docs/demo/starting-elpis.webp)\\n![Starting Codex with the same prompt](docs/demo/starting-codex.webp)\\n\\nExample end state — Elpis:\\n\\n![Elpis end state](docs/demo/elpis-end-state.webp)\\n\\nExample end state — Codex:\\n\\n![Codex end state](docs/demo/codex-end-state.webp)\\n\\n
\\n\\n## Core Features\\n\\n### Context control in four layers\\n\\n| Level | What it does | When |\\n| --- | --- | --- |\\n| **1. Shell-output filtering** | Supported commands are rewritten through RTK's `PreToolUse` hook, before their output ever reaches the model. In one real investigation it removed 72–97% of three broad `rg` outputs. The installer installs [RTK](https://github.com/rtk-ai/rtk) and Elpis registers the hook on first launch, where you trust it like any other hook. | Before the agent sees it |\\n| **2. Safety cap** | Deterministic truncation bounds exceptionally large tool output. Inherited from Codex, unchanged. | Before the agent sees it |\\n| **3. Ace steady pass** | Meaning-aware. Useful results become a compact conclusion plus an evidence pointer; dead ends leave the working context entirely. Two Continuation Modes\\n\\nElpis separates the model provider's native thread from its own provider-neutral session state, which gives two ways to continue work:\\n\\n| | Exact resume | Lean continuation |\\n| :--- | :--- | :--- |\\n| **What continues** | The provider's native thread, with its accumulated history. | A fresh thread, re-anchored from portable checkpoints. |\\n| **History source** | Full native thread history (`thread_id`). | `GOAL.md` + `ES.md` + applicable rule files. |\\n| **Token footprint** | Grows with raw turn history until compaction. | Bounded by the per-source character caps in `codex-rs/core/src/elpis_context.rs`. |\\n| **Provider mobility** | Bound to the originating provider thread. | Provider-neutral — the checkpoint is plain Markdown. |\\n| **Evidence** | Provider transcript on disk. | Provider transcript on disk, plus the checkpoint. |\\n\\n> **Open decision.** The threshold at which Elpis should switch automatically from exact resume to lean continuation is listed under Deferred Decisions in [`GUIDE.md`](https://github.com/MasihMoafi/Elpis/blob/main/docs/GUIDE.md). Today the portable checkpoint is contributed to thread context on every thread start; there is no automatic tier-switching state machine.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 2. How Lean Continuation Is Delivered\\n\\nContinuity is a context contribution, not a separate replay path. `ElpisContinuityExtension` (`codex-rs/app-server/src/extensions.rs`) implements `ContextContributor`; on thread context assembly it calls `build_continuity_prompt` (`codex-rs/core/src/elpis_context.rs`) and injects the result as a separate developer prompt fragment.\\n\\n`build_continuity_prompt` reads only the sources currently admitted in the Context Ledger, so anything you toggle off in the ledger stops being carried forward on the next turn.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 3. Portable Checkpoint Layout\\n\\nPortable session state lives independently of provider threads:\\n\\n```text\\n~/.elpis/context/workspaces/<workspace>/\\n├── GOAL.md          # Active objective for this workspace\\n├── ES.md            # Session checkpoint, rewritten after each completed turn\\n└── admission.toml   # Per-source admission flags driven by the Context Ledger\\n```\\n\\nThe `<workspace>` segment is a slug derived from the working directory plus a short hash, so separate checkouts never share a checkpoint.\\n\\n### `GOAL.md`\\n\\nWritten by `write_goal` (`codex-rs/tui/src/elpis_context.rs`):\\n\\n```markdown\\n# Elpis Goal\\n\\n- Workspace: `/path/to/project`\\n- Thread: `<thread_id>`\\n- Status: <status>\\n- Updated: <unix_timestamp>\\n\\n## Objective\\n\\n<objective text>\\n```\\n\\n### `ES.md`\\n\\nWritten by `write_session_checkpoint` in the same module, from the completed turn's own items — command executions and patch applications — rather than from a model-generated summary:\\n\\n```markdown\\n# Elpis Session Checkpoint\\n\\n- Workspace: `/path/to/project`\\n- Thread: `<thread_id>`\\n- Turn: `<turn_id>`\\n- Status: <status>\\n- Updated: <unix_timestamp>\\n- Goal: [GOAL.md](GOAL.md) when present\\n\\n## Latest Result\\n\\n<final agent message for the turn, or \\"No final agent result was recorded.\\">\\n\\n## Changed Files\\n\\n- `path/to/file.rs` (modified)\\n\\n## Commands\\n\\n- `cargo test` (exit 0)\\n\\n## Exact Evidence\\n\\n- Full turn remains in the provider transcript.\\n```\\n\\nBoth files are written to a temporary path and renamed into place, so a crash mid-write cannot leave a truncated checkpoint.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 4. Failure Behavior\\n\\nIf writing `ES.md` fails, the turn still completes: Elpis logs a warning and surfaces `Turn completed, but Elpis could not save ES.md: <error>` in the transcript (`codex-rs/tui/src/app/app_server_events.rs`). Continuity degrades visibly rather than silently, but it does not abort the turn.\\n\\n\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 5. Related Surfaces\\n\\n- **Context admission** — which checkpoint sources are carried forward is controlled in the Context Ledger; see [Context](context.md).\\n- **Memory** — durable cross-session facts live in `MEMORY.md`, switchable in the Context Ledger.\\n- **Providers** — because checkpoints are plain Markdown, switching provider mid-task does not discard them; see [Providers](providers.md).\\n"}]

Be Elpis, my friend.\\n\\nElpis is the environment an agent enters and assimilates into. The selected model or agent runtime may change, but the user's goals, working style, durable knowledge, context policy, evidence, and behavioral boundaries continue coherently. Elpis is both a state and a direction: it is never fully complete, and each verified change should make the environment clearer, more capable, and easier for its creator to control.\\n\\n## Purpose\\n\\nElpis is a provider-neutral coding-agent TUI. It does not try to make a new foundation model. It gives agents backed by OpenAI/Codex, Gemini, Claude, or another model one coherent local interface by managing:\\n\\n- instructions and project knowledge admitted into working context;\\n- the boundary between transient context and durable memory;\\n- tools, edits, commands, permissions, and their evidence;\\n- continuity across turns, compaction, and sessions;\\n- a model-independent TUI where consequential actions remain inspectable.\\n\\nThe intended result is assimilation: whichever model provider is selected, the agent adopts the user's harness, workspace, memory, and control policy without being buried under them.\\n\\n## Product Value\\n\\nElpis should create value in five ways:\\n\\n1. **Assimilation:** a selected runtime adopts the creator's applicable instructions, goals, context, memory, and behavioral rules, rather than the user adapting to it.\\n2. **Context sovereignty:** the user can see and control what enters the agent's working set. Selecting a file is an intentional context operation, not decoration.\\n3. **Reliable continuity:** sessions preserve goals, decisions, changes, and evidence across model changes, compaction, and restarts, while disposable logs and stale file bodies fall away instead of replaying an ever-growing transcript.\\n4. **Safe, transparent agency:** edits and commands use explicit sandbox and approval contracts. The UI shows what is proposed and records what happened; Elpis does not claim success when it has only hidden or documented a gap.\\n5. **Runtime choice and user ownership:** Elpis keeps one surrounding control environment while allowing the model provider and low-level agent runtime to change explicitly. Durable state is inspectable, editable, exportable, and not tied to one provider or runtime.\\n\\nElpis is not primarily a provider switcher, transcript viewer, or collection of slash commands. It is not distinguished by having another terminal chat interface. Existing projects already provide strong model access, tools, permissions, terminal rendering, and agent loops; Elpis reuses those implementations and is distinguished by the five values above.\\n\\n## Desired Output\\n\\nShip an installable terminal product, not a repository demo, in which a user can:\\n\\n1. authenticate and deliberately select a supported model and runtime;\\n2. see which runtime owns the turn and which capabilities Elpis retains;\\n3. give the agent a task under Read Only, Default, or Full Access permissions;\\n4. watch readable commands, output, file changes, diffs, failures, and verification;\\n5. inspect and control the exact working context admitted by Elpis;\\n6. resume later from the same goal, decisions, changes, and relevant memory without replaying irrelevant history;\\n7. switch to at least one non-Codex runtime while retaining Elpis-owned continuity;\\n8. install and complete a real coding task from a clean environment.\\n\\nThe product succeeds only when these behaviors pass their acceptance checks and the distinctive context/continuity behavior is demonstrably useful compared with the selected runtime alone.\\n\\n## Proof Standard\\n\\nA feature is real only when its user-visible acceptance check passes and the evidence is recorded. Documentation, hidden code, or a plausible architecture is not proof. `TASKS.md` is the current-state record against this standard.\\n\\nThe defining evaluation is whether a fresh supported runtime can enter Elpis, receive the right current goal and relevant history, obey creator rules, perform visible work under the chosen permission mode, and resume later without irrelevant context.\\n\\n## Requirements\\n\\nThis section preserves confirmed product requirements. Current implementation state belongs in `TASKS.md`, not here.\\n\\n### Working Agreement\\n\\n- Keep required work ahead of speculative features.\\n- Challenge unnecessary complexity and solution-first requests.\\n- Record evidence rather than confidence.\\n- Prefer small, reversible changes and the smallest useful verification.\\n\\n### Task Importance and Task Difficulty\\n\\nElpis product tasks use three importance levels:\\n\\n- **Foundational:** Elpis loses its purpose, reliability, or basic usability without it.\\n- **Important:** a material improvement after the foundation is solid.\\n- **Nice-to-have:** optional work that cannot delay foundational polish.\\n\\nThese levels are not release numbers and do not describe implementation complexity.\\n\\nEasy, Medium, and Hard are separate difficulty labels. They describe how much reasoning, coordination, and architectural judgment a task requires and may be used by future automatic model routing such as `/auto`.\\n\\n### Confirmed Requirements\\n\\n**R1. Provider-neutral Elpis environment** — Elpis owns the TUI, provider/runtime selection, context projection, durable memory, provider-neutral continuity, behavioral policy, permissions bridge, and evidence. A selected runtime may own its low-level model loop and native tools, but authentication must never silently transfer Elpis-owned state or product identity to that runtime.\\n\\n**R2. Visible and controlled agency** — Commands and file changes follow explicit permission and sandbox policies. The interface must preserve changed paths, diffs, command status, failures, and verification evidence.\\n\\n**R3. Deliberate context lifecycle** — Elpis must know what the model receives. Rules, goal, selected files, conversation, tool output, and memory have visible sources, sizes, reasons, and lifetimes. Stale exploration leaves the next request only after its useful conclusion and exact evidence pointer are retained. A length threshold alone is not a complete context policy.\\n\\n**R4. Exact and lean continuity** — The active goal, decisions, constraints, changed files, verification, blockers, and next action survive restarts. Elpis supports exact native-thread resume and lean continuation from a compact portable checkpoint.\\n\\n**R5. Curated memory** — Memory stores reusable facts and proven procedures, not transcripts. Promotion requires repeated useful recall across distinct contexts. Memory remains searchable, attributable, reviewable, deletable, and bounded. Deleted or faded facts enter a searchable archive before baseline reset; archive failure must stop the reset.\\n\\n**R6. Enforceable creator and project rules** — Applicable `AGENTS.md`, project requirements, and behavioral rules reach the model and action layer. Hard safety rules are enforced by code where prompts are insufficient.\\n\\n**R7. Claims require proof** — Documentation separates implemented behavior, remote tests, and outstanding user acceptance. Design documents and hidden code are not proof.\\n\\n**R8. Expensive capabilities are plugged in, not built in** — Elpis ships no retrieval or speech engine and no model weights. It must insert editable text and must not auto-submit it.\\n- Do not add slash commands unless Masih explicitly selects them.\\n\\n### Deferred Decisions\\n\\n- Whether goal changes require explicit confirmation.\\n- Default threshold for switching from exact to lean continuation.\\n- `/auto`, dreaming reports, richer animation, voice integration details, and scheduled work.\\n\\n## Source Map\\n\\nTreat upstream behavior as evidence, not inspiration copied from memory.\\n\\n### Codex: Execution and Interface Reference\\n\\nPrimary source is the local sibling clone at `~/Desktop/p/codex`; its origin is [openai/codex](https://github.com/openai/codex). Use the local committed source when it can answer the question.\\n\\nImportant areas:\\n\\n- app-server and protocol: `codex-rs/app-server`, `codex-rs/app-server-protocol`;\\n- Rust TUI: `codex-rs/tui`;\\n- core runtime: `codex-rs/core`.\\n\\nCodex is the contained implementation foundation for thread/turn semantics, streaming, file changes, commands, approvals, sandboxing, sessions, and TUI ergonomics.
